column1: What three operations are forbidden in interrupt (atomic) context in a Linux driver?
column2: Sleeping, allocating memory with GFP_KERNEL, and acquiring mutexes — only spinlocks and atomic operations are permitted.

column1: Why must MMIO register access use readl()/writel() instead of raw pointer dereferences?
column2: Because the compiler's store-reordering and caching rules don't apply to device memory; these barrier-enforcing accessors guarantee ordering and volatility that raw pointers do not.

column1: What is the key architectural difference between Port I/O and Memory-Mapped I/O?
column2: Port I/O uses a dedicated x86 64KB I/O address space accessed via IN/OUT instructions; MMIO maps device registers into the normal physical address space, accessed via standard load/store instructions.

column1: What is the 'Atomic ISR, Deferred Work' invariant?
column2: An ISR must execute in interrupt context (non-sleepable, microsecond-scale) and cannot do heavy processing; all substantial work (buffer processing, protocol parsing) must be deferred to a softirq, tasklet, or workqueue.

column1: What does Invariant 1 (Serialized Ownership) in driver protocols require for DMA buffers?
column2: At any instant, either the CPU or the device exclusively owns a DMA buffer; ownership must be explicitly transferred via dma_map_single()/dma_unmap_single() or descriptor ring state transitions, never implicitly shared.

column1: What is Command-Completion Atomicity (Invariant 2) in driver protocols?
column2: Every command issued to a device must map to exactly one completion event (status poll, interrupt, or descriptor writeback); orphaned commands cause leaked memory and potential kernel panics.

column1: In the ioctl contract, what four steps occur before the driver's .unlocked_ioctl handler executes?
column2: 1) VFS validates the fd and resolves file_operations, 2) kernel performs capability checks (e.g., CAP_NET_ADMIN), 3) the command number's _IOC/_IOR/_IOW/_IOWR encoding determines direction/size, 4) kernel copies data via copy_from_user()/copy_to_user() so the driver never touches raw user pointers.

column1: Why can't a driver hardcode physical addresses for device resources (Invariant 1 — Device Independence)?
column2: Because the bus subsystem (PCI, USB, platform, etc.) enumerates devices and matches drivers dynamically; drivers must obtain resources via platform_get_resource() or pci_resource_start(), allowing one driver binary to support many hardware SKUs.

column1: What is the difference between Coherent DMA and Streaming DMA?
column2: Coherent DMA relies on hardware cache-snooping to auto-maintain CPU/device memory view consistency; Streaming DMA requires the driver to explicitly synchronize ownership using barriers and cache operations for one-directional transfers.

column1: What is Bounce Buffering used for in DMA?
column2: It's used when a device can only address a limited physical memory range (e.g., 24-bit bus); the kernel allocates intermediate buffers in reachable memory and copies data to/from the actual target buffer.

column1: Why is the kernel's direct physical memory mapping (used by kmalloc) faster than vmalloc's address range?
column2: The direct mapping translates virtual-to-physical via simple offset subtraction (__pa()) with no TLB miss overhead, since it's physically contiguous; vmalloc maps virtually contiguous but physically discontiguous pages, requiring page table walks.

column1: What is the core asymmetry a device driver must bridge between hardware and kernel?
column2: Hardware speaks in physical addresses, edge-triggered signals, and timed command sequences, while the kernel speaks in virtual addresses, process contexts, and synchronization primitives — the driver translates between these two worlds.
